title: GRPO groups, normalization and KL estimators

key_terms.GRPO: Group-relative policy optimization, which normalizes rewards within a group of responses to the same prompt.
key_terms.Group baseline: The group mean reward subtracted from each response's reward in place of a learned value baseline.
key_terms.Zero-variance group: A group with identical rewards, assigned zero advantages by an explicit policy to avoid division by zero.
key_terms.Length normalization: The averaging convention for token terms; per-response averaging weights responses equally, while pooling all tokens favors longer responses.
key_terms.KL estimator: A sample average whose expectation equals KL(p, q) only when actions are drawn from p; old-policy samples need importance correction.

outcome: Compute group-relative advantages, expose degeneracy and weighting choices, and identify the sampling law required by a KL estimator.
verification: Shifting all rewards leaves the normalized advantages unchanged, a constant group yields zero advantages, response and token averaging give 0 and 1/3, the estimator differs from current-policy KL under the wrong sampling law, and its value 0 has derivative 0.5.

exercises.title: Shift all rewards
exercises.hint: Both the mean and every reward shift together.
exercises.answer: Relative normalization removes a common level; it does not preserve information about absolute task success.

reasoning.why: The mean is 1.5 and the centered rewards are [-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5]. Their root mean square is the square root of 1.25, about 1.118, giving advantages about [-1.342, -0.447, 0.447, 1.342]. Adding 10 shifts the mean by 10 and leaves the centered values unchanged.
reasoning.pitfall: Reading normalized advantages as task success is the mistake. A group scoring 10 to 13 and one scoring 0 to 3 look identical after normalization.
reasoning.verify: Case A asserts mean 0, mean square 1 and equality with both the shifted and the doubled group. The exercise checks assert that reversing the group negates the advantages.

exercises.title: Inspect a constant group
exercises.task: Compare all-zero and all-one reward groups.
exercises.expected: Both produce zero relative advantages under the declared rule.
exercises.answer: These groups represent different absolute outcomes despite the same lack of within-group ranking signal.

reasoning.why: Centering gives all zeros and the scale is 0, so the helper returns zeros instead of dividing by zero. Both groups produce no learning signal even though one failed every attempt and the other succeeded every time.
reasoning.pitfall: Dividing by a small epsilon instead of handling zero scale returns zeros too, but adding epsilon to every scale changes the advantages of other groups slightly. Also, treating all-success and all-failure groups as equivalent in a report hides absolute performance.
reasoning.verify: Case A asserts `group_advantages([0, 0, 0]).tolist() == [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]` and prints the constant group `[1, 1]`. Track the share of constant groups separately.

exercises.title: Change length weighting
exercises.task: Give advantages-1,+1 to responses of length 2,4.
exercises.answer: A token average weights longer responses more heavily and defines a different objective from equal-response weighting.

reasoning.approach: Take advantages -1 and +1 for responses of 2 and 4 tokens. Average per response and per token.
reasoning.why: The response average is (-1 + 1) / 2 = 0. The token average is (-1 times 2 + 1 times 4) / 6 = 2 / 6 = 1 / 3. The longer response has twice the influence under token averaging.
reasoning.pitfall: Treating the reduction as an implementation detail is the mistake. A token average rewards length when long responses carry positive advantage, so the two choices optimize different objectives.

exercises.title: Check the sampling law
exercises.task: Average case B KL terms under the old uniform policy.
exercises.expected: The value differs from current-policy KL.
exercises.hint: The identity requires expectation under the numerator policy p.
exercises.answer: Importance correction can recover the value expectation with adequate support, but has variance costs and does not by itself prove a gradient estimator is correct.

reasoning.approach: With p = [0.8, 0.2] and q = [0.5, 0.5], compute `kl_terms(p, q)` and average it under p, under old = [0.5, 0.5], and under old with weights p / old.
reasoning.why: The ratios q / p are 0.625 and 2.5, giving terms about 0.095 and 0.584. Under p the average is about 0.193, the exact KL 0.8 log 1.6 + 0.2 log 0.4. Under old it is about 0.339, which is wrong. Reweighting by p / old recovers 0.193.
reasoning.pitfall: Averaging over samples drawn from the old policy without correction is the mistake. The estimator assumes samples from the current policy.
reasoning.verify: Case B asserts all terms are nonnegative, `p @ terms` equals the exact KL, `old @ terms` does not, and the importance-weighted average does.

exercises.title: Separate value from derivative
exercises.task: Evaluate the centered two-action surrogate at zero log odds.
exercises.expected: Its value is 0 while its derivative is 0.5.
exercises.hint: Each centered advantage multiplies a different probability derivative.
exercises.answer: A zero average advantage or initial objective value does not imply absence of a learning signal.

reasoning.approach: Define the two-action surrogate 2 times sigmoid(delta) - 1 and evaluate its value and its central difference at delta 0.
reasoning.why: The value is 2 times 0.5 - 1 = 0. The derivative is 2 times sigmoid'(0) = 2 times 0.25 = 0.5. A zero value at the start does not mean a zero gradient.
reasoning.pitfall: Concluding that training is stuck because the initial objective or mean advantage is zero is the mistake. Normalized advantages always average zero, yet they still produce gradients.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts `surrogate(0) == 0` and that the central difference with h = 1e-5 is 0.5 within 1e-10.

exercises.title: Declare algorithm variants
exercises.task: Change standard-deviation correction, epsilon or token reduction.
exercises.expected: Record the change as part of the training algorithm.
exercises.hint: These settings alter advantage or gradient weighting.
exercises.answer: A shared acronym is insufficient to establish that two implementations optimize the same objective.

reasoning.approach: Record each implementation choice as part of the algorithm name or config: standard deviation correction, clip epsilon, KL estimator and token or response reduction.
reasoning.why: Exercises 1 to 4 show that these choices change the advantages, the weights and the KL estimate. Two runs called by the same acronym can optimize measurably different objectives.
reasoning.pitfall: Comparing results across papers or codebases because they share an algorithm name is the mistake. Differences may come from these unreported choices, not from the claimed contribution.
reasoning.verify: No reference assertion covers this task. Diff the configuration of two runs before comparing results, and list every differing field in the comparison.
